*Note: this post was generated by Claude (an AI) as test content for this site.*

Menger's theorem is one of the basic results of graph theory. It says that "how many vertices you must delete to cut A off from B" and "how many disjoint paths run from A to B" are always the same number. This post states it precisely and goes through the short proof by Frank Göring (2000), in the form given in Diestel's *Graph Theory*, Theorem 3.3.1.

## Definitions

Let G = (V, E) be a finite undirected graph, and let A, B ⊆ V be two sets of vertices (they may overlap).

- An **A–B path** is a path P = x₀x₁…xₖ whose first vertex is the only vertex of P in A, and whose last vertex is the only vertex of P in B. In symbols: V(P) ∩ A = {x₀} and V(P) ∩ B = {xₖ}. A single vertex in A ∩ B counts as an A–B path of length 0.
- Paths are **disjoint** if they have no vertex in common.
- A set X ⊆ V **separates A from B** (is an **A–B separator**) if every A–B path contains a vertex of X. For example, A and B are both A–B separators.

One fact used several times below: any walk that starts in A and ends in B contains an A–B path. (Take the last vertex of the walk in A, then the first vertex after it in B, and shorten the walk between them to a path.)

## The theorem

> **Theorem (Menger, 1927).** Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph and A, B ⊆ V. Then the minimum number of vertices in an A–B separator equals the maximum number of disjoint A–B paths in G.

The classic special case: if s and t are two non-adjacent vertices, then the minimum number of vertices (other than s and t) whose removal disconnects s from t equals the maximum number of s–t paths that share no vertex except s and t. This follows by applying the theorem to A = N(s) and B = N(t), the neighbourhoods of s and t.

## Proof

Let k be the minimum size of an A–B separator.

### The easy direction: at most k disjoint paths

Fix an A–B separator X with |X| = k. Every A–B path contains a vertex of X. If the paths are disjoint, they contain *different* vertices of X. So there are at most |X| = k disjoint A–B paths.

### The hard direction: k disjoint paths exist

We use induction on the number of edges of G.

**Base case: G has no edges.** Then the only A–B paths are single vertices in A ∩ B. Every A–B separator must contain all of A ∩ B, and A ∩ B itself separates A from B, so k = |A ∩ B|. The vertices of A ∩ B are k disjoint A–B paths.

**Induction step.** Suppose G has an edge e = xy, and assume for contradiction that G has fewer than k disjoint A–B paths.

**Step 1: contract e.** Let G/e be the graph obtained by merging x and y into a single new vertex vₑ. In G/e we count vₑ as a member of A if x or y is in A, and as a member of B if x or y is in B.

G/e also has fewer than k disjoint A–B paths. Indeed, if G/e had k of them, then "un-contracting" vₑ (replacing it by x, y, or the edge xy, whichever is needed) turns them into k disjoint walks in G, each going from A to B. Each such walk contains an A–B path, and these paths are still disjoint, a contradiction.

G/e has fewer edges than G, so by induction G/e has an A–B separator Y with |Y| < k.

**Step 2: build a separator X in G of size exactly k.** The separator Y must contain vₑ. Otherwise Y is a set of vertices of G, and it would separate A from B in G: contracting e in any A–B path of G gives a walk in G/e from A to B, which meets Y in some vertex other than vₑ, and that vertex already lies on the original path. Then G would have an A–B separator of size less than k, contradicting the choice of k.

So set X = (Y \ {vₑ}) ∪ {x, y}. This X separates A from B in G (any A–B path that avoided X would also avoid Y after contracting e), so |X| ≥ k. On the other hand |X| ≤ |Y| + 1 ≤ k. Hence **|X| = k**.

**Step 3: k disjoint A–X paths and k disjoint X–B paths.** Now look at the graph G − e, which is G with the edge e deleted (but x and y kept).

*Claim:* every A–X separator in G − e also separates A from B in G.

Take any A–B path P in G. It meets X (because X separates A from B in G). Let z be the first vertex of P in X, and let P′ be the part of P from its start up to z. Then P′ is an A–X path. It does not use the edge e: if it did, both x and y would lie on P′, but P′ contains only one vertex of X, namely its last vertex z. So P′ is an A–X path in G − e. Any A–X separator of G − e meets P′, and hence meets P. This proves the claim.

By the claim, every A–X separator in G − e has at least k vertices. Since G − e has fewer edges than G, the induction hypothesis gives **k disjoint A–X paths in G − e**. By the same argument with the roles of A and B swapped, there are also **k disjoint X–B paths in G − e**.

**Step 4: glue them together.** Since |X| = k, each vertex of X is the end of exactly one of the A–X paths and the start of exactly one of the X–B paths.

An A–X path Q and an X–B path R can only meet inside X. If they shared a vertex v outside X, then following Q from A to v and then R from v to B would give a walk from A to B that avoids X entirely (Q meets X only at its last vertex and R only at its first). That walk would contain an A–B path avoiding X, which is impossible.

So for each vertex of X, joining its A–X path with its X–B path gives a path from A to B, and it contains an A–B path. Paths for different vertices of X are disjoint: an A–X path and an X–B path can only meet in X, and each of them contains just one vertex of X, which belongs to a different pair. This gives k disjoint A–B paths in G, contradicting our assumption.

So G has k disjoint A–B paths, which completes the induction. ∎

## Why I like this proof

Most proofs of Menger's theorem go through augmenting paths, as in the max-flow min-cut theorem. This one avoids all of that: it only contracts one edge and deletes one edge, and the induction hypothesis does the rest. The key trick is Step 2, which turns a "too small" separator in G/e into a separator in G of size exactly k, splitting the problem into an A side and a B side.

## References

- K. Menger, "Zur allgemeinen Kurventheorie", *Fundamenta Mathematicae* 10 (1927), 96–115.
- F. Göring, "Short proof of Menger's theorem", *Discrete Mathematics* 219 (2000), 295–296.
- R. Diestel, *Graph Theory*, Springer, Theorem 3.3.1.
